newsitem.title: USA: U.S. scientist shaken by Nobel award.
newsitem.headline: U.S. scientist shaken by Nobel award.

text.p: For Robert Richardson, the phone call telling him that he won the Nobel Prize for Physics on Wednesday was bittersweet.
"My first reaction was concern for my wife and daughter," he said. "It was a phone call at the same time of the morning that I found out my daughter was dead."

The Cornell University professor's eyes glistened as he recalled the pre-dawn phone call from Vanderbilt University in Tennessee nearly two years ago telling him his daughter Pamela, attending graduate school there, had died suddenly of heart failure.
His wife, Betty, is a physics lecturer at Cornell, in Ithaca, New York, and his other daughter, Jennifer, lives in Brooklyn, New York, where she plays violin in a rock band.

This time, the phone call was shocking in a different way. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced that Richardson, 59, won the 1996 Nobel Physics Prize along with two colleagues, David Lee of Cornell and Douglas Osheroff, now at Stamford University in California.

They discovered the helium isotope helium-3 can be made superfluid at a temperature only about two thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Superfluidity is a scientific term for when a liquid is made so cold it loses all its usual molecular patterns.

A research team seeking to confirm the existence of cosmic strings -- immense objects thought to have been responsible for the creation of the universe -- was able to test its theories using the three men's discovery.

"It's not something you are going to find in your kitchen," he said of the superfluid helium-3. It is, however, an important scientific tool. A California scientist is testing it to detect abrupt changes in the rotation of the earth, for instance.
"It was a suprise," Richardson said of the Nobel news when he was interviewed during a break from a National Research Council panel meeting in Washington on condensed matter and the study of liquids.

"I knew it was an important discovery and was much talked about 10 to 15 years ago," he said. But he has paid little attention to the possibility that his work in the early 1970s would earn him the coveted Nobel Prize.
"It was something we just didn't talk about," he said, not even at the dinner table with his wife. "Maybe it was something to do with a jinx," he laughed.
He said the desk clerk at his hotel brought him down to earth. His wife, unable to reach him by phone, left a simple message: "Congratulations."
"When the desk clerk told me, he asked if I had won the lottery," Richardson said. "No, I told him the Nobel Prize. 'What's that?', he said."
